title: RIAA CEO Talks Midterms, AI Deepfakes and Trump: ‘Music Is a Very Bipartisan Issue’
summary: On the latest episode of Billboard On the Record, RIAA CEO/chairman Mitch Glazier talks Napster and AI and why he's confident the NO FAKES Act will pass soon.
contentText:
There is a lot going on in Washington D.C. Between conflicts in the Middle East, rising inflation and other hot button issues, it could be understandable if music industry issues fall lower on the priority list for politicians these days.

However, no matter what is going on in the nation’s capitol, it’s the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and its chairman/CEO Mitch Glazier ‘s mission to get the D.C. power players to pay attention to causes related to the recorded music industry, and he tells Billboard it’s actually not as hard as one might believe. “Everyone loves music,” Glazier says with a smile and a shrug.

To build rapport, Glazier is known to ask members of Congress about the song they danced to at their weddings, tugging on the emotional heartstrings of both Republicans and Democrats alike, before launching into RIAA talking points about strengthening copyright protection and safeguarding against AI deepfake impersonation.

His biggest push right now is the NO FAKES Act, a bill guarding against unauthorized deepfakes, that’s been reintroduced to the House and Senate for several years in the row, each time adding in new supporters, ranging from Google and OpenAI to SAG-AFTRA and the Motion Picture Association.

Last week, Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) took the bill to the senate floor for a vote, and while it received nearly universal support, it was thwarted by one dissenter, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who expressed concern that the bill did not have sufficient exceptions for the use of one’s image in satire or political commentary.

With the midterm election — and the holidays — fast approaching, it is looking like the bill may need to go through another round of reintroduction in 2027. Still, as Glazier puts it, he’s “an optimistic person,” and he believes there’s still a possibility that the bill could get unanimous support during the lame duck period and slip through in the final moments of 2026. “This is one that has such broad support, both from a coalition basis and from members of Congress — House, Senate, Republican, Democrat — that if we can work out a couple of these last issues, I think it has a real shot at what we call unanimous consent,” he says.

To talk through the upcoming election, Trump’s second term and coalition building for music rights on Capitol Hill, Glazier joins the latest episode of Billboard On the Record .

To watch this episode of  Billboard On the Record , check out the YouTube video below or click  here  for more viewing and listening options. An edited and condensed excerpt of the conversation can also be found below.

Since you have your feet in both words, how would you compare D.C. and Hollywood?

There are a lot of similarities. D.C. is all about a brand around a person, right? And an artist is all about a brand around a person. They all have teams, and it’s not like you’re working for, you know, Coca-Cola, the corporation. You’re working for this senator. You’re working for this congressman. It’s about them, their views — what they want to put out to the world. And your job is to make sure that what they want to get out there, they get out there successfully, and then you try to help with the reaction to what they put out there. Also, the fact that politics and entertainment and music are dinner table topics — everybody is interested in that. Families fight over these two subjects at Thanksgiving.

The stakes are a little bit different, I will say.

Depends on the family!

With everything going on in D.C., there are a ton of hot-button issues that are very important right now. Is it difficult to get people to pay attention to music-related issues?

It’s not, because we’re music and everybody loves music. I mean, the first thing I ask any person who’s elected to Congress is, “What was the song that you danced to at your wedding?” Only music can bring you back immediately to something in your life that’s incredibly important. And when they think about it and they answer, you’re like, “Music’s important, and it needs to be protected.” Then, I run into how the Constitution actually gives them the job to do, and that they’re bound to do it under law, and that they have to secure rights, and I go through the whole thing. But we always start with music. That is our secret weapon because this industry is small with a huge impact on American culture. We don’t have the revenues that AI companies have, tech companies have, even that other entertainment industries have. Still, I would argue that we are the most impactful industry with the least amount of revenue.

Do you find that you guys have more success advocating for these issues with folks who consider themselves to be Republicans or Democrats?

Unlike many other industries, it does not break down by party. Music is a very bipartisan issue. I would say that there are arguments that you might lean on more or less, depending on the audience. So, for example, a lot of Republicans support the music industry because they believe in property rights, and they want to make sure that this constitutionally given property right is protected. It’s also individual freedom and the ability to sort of negotiate freely with property that you have, and free speech issues. And then on the Democratic side, although they also very much care about those issues, they also care about workers’ issues, and now the Republican side also cares about those issues, so it’s very bipartisan. We might emphasize one thing more than another, but for the most part, it breaks down a little bit more by geography than it does by party.

As politics has gotten more divided and more extreme, how has that affected the way that you have to go after and convince these politicians to pay attention to these issues.

So weirdly, it brings them together. At the end of the day, they are human beings. They actually do crave working together, even though it’s seemingly more impossible these days. So when we have a hearing on music, it’s almost like this big sigh of relief. The members come; they’re nice to each other. They care about it. They defer to each other. It’s almost like they’ve been dying to actually be normal and nice to each other, and we present that opportunity for them. Also, almost every event that we do is bipartisan. So we bring them together with music and help them get to know each other and their families and their friends. Music brings out the humanity in people

How would you compare working with the Trump administration in his second term versus his first?

I would say that generally, this administration stems from the top. It’s unlike the George W. Bush administration, which was sort of more bottom-up. Also, the president loves music — absolutely loves music.

He does?

He takes out his Spotify playlist. He shows people: “What do you think?” He listens, but they don’t publish his playlist. [Former President] Obama published his playlist, so we got to see more from him, but anecdotally, from folks who have been with [Trump], he’s like showing people songs a lot of times. I think it’s something that was pushed to him in an algorithm he listened to. He’s like, “Hey, have you heard this?“ It’s more like a discovery thing.

I mean, I know everyone loves music. It’s just odd to think of Trump having a personal life.

I love the fact that [former President] Biden and Trump and Obama have nothing in common, really…but all three of them love music. 

When I talk to people about generative AI, sometimes they’ll say, “Generative AI is music’s next Napster moment.” I’m wondering…
